system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Non-standard model of arithmetic
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Definition of standard versus non-standard structures for LA, the existence of countable non-standard models by compactness, the block structure of non-standard elements in models of PA (ordered like the rationals), contrast with models of Q and PA2. Excludes Tennenbaum's theorem proof, which is only stated.

ATOMS:
- CS-COMP-C08-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: A structure $\mathfrak{M}$ for the language of arithmetic $\mathcal{L}_A$ is non-standard if and only if it is not isomorphic to the standard model $\mathfrak{N}$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0178-s02] We call a structure for LA standard if it is isomorphic to N.
    [CS-COMP-p0178-s03] If a structure isn’t isomorphic to N, it is called non-standard.
    [CS-COMP-p0178-s04] Definition 7.15. A structure M for LA is non-standard if it is not isomorphic to N.
- CS-COMP-C08-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: In a structure $M$ for $\mathcal{L}_A$, an element $x \in |M|$ that equals $\mathrm{Val}^M(\overline{n})$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ is called a standard number of $M$, and an element that does not is called a non-standard number.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0178-s05] The elements x ∈|M| which are equal to ValM(n) for some n ∈N are called standard numbers (of M), and those not, non-standard numbers.
- CS-COMP-C08-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: A non-standard structure for $\mathcal{L}_A$ must contain at least one non-standard element, and conversely the existence of a non-standard element in a structure for $\mathcal{L}_A$ guarantees that the structure is non-standard.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0178-s06] By Proposition 7.12, any standard structure for LA contains only standard elements.
    [CS-COMP-p0178-s07] Consequently, a non-standard structure must contain at least one non-standard element.
- CS-COMP-C08-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: The theory $\mathrm{TA} = \{A : \mathfrak{N} \models A\}$ of the standard model $\mathfrak{N}$ has a countable non-standard model, which can be shown with the compactness theorem.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0179-s01] Proposition 7.17. Let TA = {A : N ⊨A} be the theory of N.
    [CS-COMP-p0179-s02] TA has a countable non-standard model.
- CS-COMP-C08-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: If a non-standard model $M$ of $\mathrm{PA}$ is countable, every non-standard element lies in a block of non-standard elements ordered like $\mathbb{Z}$ by $<^M$, and these blocks are themselves arranged like $\mathbb{Q}$, with no smallest block, no largest block, and always a block between any two blocks.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0189-s17] If a non-standard model M of PA is countable, every non-standard element is part of a “block” of non-standard elements which are ordered like Z by <M.
    [CS-COMP-p0189-s18] These blocks themselves are arranged like Q, i.e., there is no smallest or largest block, and there is always a block in between any two blocks.
- CS-COMP-C08-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: In a model $\mathfrak{M}$ of PA, the block of a non-standard element $x$ is the set of those $y \in |\mathfrak{M}|$ such that $x \oplus n = y$ or $y \oplus n = x$ for some standard $n$, and this block has no least and no greatest element.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0184-s01] Proposition 7.23. Every nonstandard element x of |M| is an element of the subset
    [CS-COMP-p0184-s02] We call this subset the block of x and write it as [x].
    [CS-COMP-p0184-s03] It has no least and no greatest element.
    [CS-COMP-p0184-s04] It can be characterized as the set of those y ∈|M| such that, for some standard n, x ⊕n = y or y ⊕n = x.
- CS-COMP-C08-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: Two countable non-standard models $M_1$ and $M_2$ of true arithmetic have isomorphic reducts to the language containing only $<$ and $=$, yet it does not follow that they are isomorphic in the full language of arithmetic, because isomorphism is relative to a language and there are non-isomorphic ways to define addition and multiplication over $|M_1|$ and $|M_2|$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0186-s07] It follows that for any two countable non-standard models M1 and M2 of true arithmetic, their reducts to the language containing < and = only are isomorphic.
    [CS-COMP-p0186-s10] Note that it does not follow that 𝔐1 and 𝔐2 are isomorphic in the full language of arithmetic (indeed, isomorphism is always relative to a language), as there are non-isomorphic ways to define addition and multiplication over |M1| and |M2|.
- CS-COMP-C08-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: The theory $\mathrm{Q}$ has models in which $\forall x \forall y\,(x+y)=(y+x)$ is false, but such models cannot also be models of $\mathrm{TA}$ or of $\mathrm{PA}$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0179-s19] Q is much weaker than TA, e.g., Q ⊬∀x ∀y (x + y) = (y + x).
    [CS-COMP-p0179-s20] Weaker theories are easier to satisfy: they have more models.
    [CS-COMP-p0179-s21] E.g., Q has models which make ∀x ∀y (x + y) = (y + x) false, but those cannot also be models of TA, or PA for that matter.
- CS-COMP-C08-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: Models of the weaker theory Q can contain as few as a single non-standard number, but such simple structures are not models of PA or of TA.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-COMP-p0182-s11] How many are there? We’ve seen that models of the weaker theory Q can contain as few as a single non-standard number.
    [CS-COMP-p0182-s12] But these simple structures are not models of PA or TA.
